title: Intel Xeon 658X Review: Granite Rapids For Workstations
gist: Intel brings Granite Rapids silicon to workstations as the rebranded Xeon 600 family, pushing core counts to 86 (up 43%) with Redwood Cove cores, more PCIe lanes and MRDIMM support, but with single-threaded gains of only ~9% versus 61% multi-threaded. The update ends a three-year workstation stagnation and squares Intel off against AMD Threadripper.

themes.theme: Xeon workstation rebrand and end of stagnation

insights.claim: Intel has replaced its longstanding Xeon W-2xxx/W-3xxx workstation branding with a 'Xeon 600' scheme derived from its Xeon 6 server brand for the new Granite Rapids workstation chips.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Branding alignment signals Intel is folding workstation into its server roadmap cadence, which matters for tracking future refresh timing.
insights.quote: it has been replaced by a variant of the branding Intel uses for its server chips, the Xeon 6 brand, giving rise to the Xeon 600 branding for their newest workstation chips.

insights.claim: The Xeon 600 family is the first new workstation silicon Intel has shipped in over three years, ending a stagnation in which Intel skipped bringing Emerald Rapids to workstations and only refreshed Sapphire Rapids-based parts in 2024.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A three-year gap gave AMD Threadripper room to gain share; the refresh is Intel's attempt to reclaim the high-end workstation buyer.
insights.quote: The first new silicon for workstation processors in over three years, the Xeon 600 family is intended to deliver a modest boost to single-threaded performance and a major boost to multi-threaded performance

insights.claim: The Xeon 600 platform is characterized as the workstation lineup's 'Arrow Lake moment,' bringing all-new Redwood Cove silicon after a long run analogous to Intel's stagnant Alder Lake/Golden Cove consumer era.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Frames the release as a genuine architectural reset rather than an incremental refresh, raising the bar for what buyers should expect.
insights.quote: the Xeon 600 series represents the workstation chip lineup's Arrow Lake moment, as it means the platform is getting all-new silicon based on Intel's Redwood Cove CPU cores.

insights.claim: The top Xeon 600 chip offers 86 CPU cores, a roughly 43% increase over the prior generation's 60-core Xeon W-3500, at roughly the same peak frequency.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Core-count leadership is the main lever Intel has to compete with AMD Threadripper in embarrassingly parallel workstation workloads.
insights.quote: while the top Xeon W-3500 chip offered 60 CPU cores, the top Xeon 600 chip brings that to 86 cores, or about a 43% increase in core counts, running at roughly the same peak frequency as before.

insights.claim: Intel's own material lists single-threaded performance gains for its top SKU at just 9% versus 61% higher multi-threaded performance, so the Xeon 600's uplift comes almost entirely from additional cores.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Buyers with lightly-threaded or latency-sensitive workloads gain little; the value proposition is narrow to heavily parallel tasks.
insights.quote: listing the single-threaded performance gains for Intel's top SKU at just 9%, versus 61% higher multi-threaded performance.

insights.claim: Redwood Cove cores deliver area and power efficiency rather than a major IPC or clock-speed jump over the Raptor Cove cores they replace, and combined with the Intel 3 fab node let Intel pack far more cores per Granite Rapids die.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: The gains are a process/efficiency story, not an architecture-IPC story, which caps single-thread competitiveness against AMD.
insights.quote: What it has going for it instead are both area and power efficiency, which, combined with the use of the company's Intel 3 fab node, have allowed Intel to pack a much larger number of CPU cores into a single Granite Rapids chip.

insights.claim: Granite Rapids workstation CPUs provide a full 128 lanes of PCIe Gen5 from the host CPU, up from 112 on the prior generation, and add CXL 2.0 support enabling memory pooling and single-level switching.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: More lanes and CXL 2.0 expand accelerator and memory-expansion headroom, relevant for AI-adjacent workstation builds.
insights.quote: Intel now offers a full 128 lanes of PCIe Gen5 coming from the host CPU, which is up from 112 lanes on the previous-generation Xeons

insights.claim: The top half of the Xeon 600 series (28 cores and higher) supports Multiplexed Rank DIMMs (MRDIMMs) enabling effective memory speeds up to DDR5-8000, while all SKUs support DDR5-6400 at 1 DPC.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: MRDIMM bandwidth is gated behind higher-core SKUs, so memory-bandwidth-bound users are pushed up the stack.
insights.quote: the top half of the Xeon 600 series (28 cores and higher) also supports Multiplexed Rank DIMMs (MRDIMMs), enabling effective memory speeds up to DDR5-8000.

insights.claim: Lower-end Xeon 600 chips (16 cores and below) are limited to 80 PCIe lanes and 4 memory channels, and a minimum buy-in of 18 cores at roughly $1,199 is required to access the full complement of DDR5 memory channels and PCIe lanes.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Feature segmentation forces buyers to move up the stack to unlock platform I/O, raising effective entry cost for a full-featured workstation.
insights.quote: A minimal buy-in of 18 cores (~$1199) is required to access the remaining DDR5 memory channels and PCIe lanes.

insights.claim: The Xeon 600 stack comprises 11 SKUs from 12 to 86 cores built on low (LCC), high (HCC), and extreme (XCC) Granite Rapids-SP configurations using one or two compute tiles on a single LGA 4710 socket.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A single socket spanning all tiers simplifies platform design but the wide range means buyers must consult SKU tables to match features.
insights.quote: The complete Xeon 600 chip stack comprises 11 SKUs, with core counts ranging from 12 to 86.

insights.claim: Boxed retail SKUs include the 654, 658X, 676X, 678X, and 696X, with all X-tier chips unlocked for overclocking, but the 658X notably lacks MRDIMM support that the other X-tier chips carry.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: The reviewed 658X is an overclockable part that still omits MRDIMM, illustrating that choosing X-tier alone doesn't guarantee full platform features.
insights.quote: All of the X-tier chips, sans the 658X, also get MRDIMM support, so going X alone is not enough to get everything the platform offers.

insights.claim: Intel's Xeon workstation line has become a niche product caught between declining desktop demand and the AI-driven server boom, even as high-end workstations remain important to engineering, art, and emerging AI markets.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Positions workstation as a smaller strategic priority for Intel, which explains the slow refresh cadence and helps gauge future investment.
insights.quote: Xeon workstation chips have certainly been treated as a more niche product in recent years.

insights.claim: The Xeon 600 is explicitly positioned to face AMD's rival Threadripper processors in the high-end workstation market.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: The head-to-head against Threadripper is the key competitive frame for evaluating whether Intel's core-count push is enough.
insights.quote: We are also looking to see how well it holds up against the stiff competition from Intel's loyal opposition, AMD, and its rival Threadripper processors.

insights.claim: Intel invested essentially all of its efficiency gains into more cores at the same tier, keeping TDPs similar to the prior generation, with the top 698X and 696X at 350W base and 420W peak and the 12-core 634 at 150W base.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Flat TDP-per-tier means power infrastructure carries over, easing platform transitions for OEMs and buyers.
insights.quote: with Intel essentially investing all of their efficiency gains into providing more CPU cores at the same tier.
